row: | DOC-A.1-6 | **Alignment of alphanumeric group items (and strongly-typed group items) relative to the first item within the group**, §8.5.1.6.1 · §8.5.1.6.5, required + documented | **Always coincident.** Every alphanumeric group item, and every strongly-typed group item (a group declared by a `TYPEDEF STRONG` type, 2002 onward), starts at the same byte as the first item subordinate to it, whatever that item's class or usage: COBOL.NET never places slack bytes ahead of a group's first item, and none between items either (no automatic alignment, item 7; no alignment or implicit FILLER for SYNCHRONIZED, item 195) — the only implicit filler is the filler bits §8.5.1.6.3 itself requires after a bit data item to reach the next byte (`05 B1 PIC 1(3) USAGE BIT` followed by `05 B2 PIC X` is a 2-byte group). A group of byte-sized items is therefore exactly the sum of its subordinate items' sizes: `05 G1 PIC 9(4) COMP` followed by `05 G2 PIC X` is a 3-byte group whose first two bytes are G1, and a strongly-typed group of `9(4) COMP-5` then `X` is likewise 3 bytes. The standard's own exceptions (the group coincident with a first item that is national, boolean, message-tag, object or pointer; the type's essential characteristics preserved) hold because there is no other case. The same answer at every edition; one layout authority computes every offset and size (`RecordLayout.OffsetOf`, `RecordLayout.PhysicalWidth`). | — |

row: | DOC-A.1-8 | **ALPHABET clause — ordinal number of characters in the native coded character sets**, §12.3.7.4 GR6, required + documented | **Code-unit order: the ordinal position of a native character is its UTF-16 code unit plus one**, in BOTH native sets. The native alphanumeric and the native national coded character sets are each the 65,536 UTF-16 code units, one per character position (item 33), ordered by code-unit value: X"00" (U+0000) is ordinal 1, `"A"` is 66, X"FF" is 256, `"€"` (U+20AC) is 8,365, and U+FFFF is 65,536; the national set uses the same numbering (`N"A"` is 66). These are the ordinals FUNCTION ORD returns and FUNCTION CHAR / CHAR-NATIONAL accept whenever no ALPHABET names a different program collating sequence (`CobolIntrinsics.Ord`, `CobolIntrinsics.Char`, `CobolIntrinsics.CharNational`); an ordinal outside 1–65,536 sets EC-ARGUMENT-FUNCTION. The same numbering at every edition (the national set exists from 2002). ⚠ HIGH-VALUE and the figurative extremes are still computed over U+0000–U+00FF rather than the whole native set (kb/Work PB1093, open). | — |

row: | DOC-A.1-9 | **Alphanumeric literals — number of hexadecimal digits that map to an alphanumeric character**, §8.3.3.2.3 SR6, required + documented | **Two.** Each pair of hexadecimal digits in a hexadecimal alphanumeric literal (`X"…"`, §8.3.3.2.2 format 2) is ONE alphanumeric character whose code is the pair's value: `X"41424344"` is `"ABCD"`, `X"4a4B"` is `"JK"` (either case of A–F), and `FUNCTION LENGTH(X"414243")` is 3. row: | DOC-A.1-16 | **CALL statement — calling a non-COBOL program**, §14.9.4.4 GR3g, required + documented | **Not possible: COBOL.NET executes no non-COBOL program through CALL.** A CALL resolves only to a COBOL.NET program — one in the run unit, or a separately compiled COBOL.NET module `<program-name>.dll` in the application directory that carries the COBOL.NET module registrar (`ProgramTable.ProbeSiblingModule`). Every other target, including a .NET assembly that is present in the application directory (`CALL "Antlr4.Runtime.Standard"`) or a system library name held in an identifier, is **not located**, so GR3g's non-COBOL branch is never reached: the CALL is unsuccessful with **EC-PROGRAM-NOT-FOUND** (GR3b) and continues per GR3h — the ON EXCEPTION imperative statement when one is written (ON OVERFLOW before 2023); otherwise, with checking for EC-PROGRAM-NOT-FOUND enabled, the applicable exception declarative (item 17), and with checking not enabled (and always at 85) the run unit terminates abnormally naming EC-PROGRAM-NOT-FOUND. There is no CALL-CONVENTION directive (§7.3.9), so a program cannot be declared non-COBOL either (item 19); program-name formation and locating for non-COBOL programs (items 13 and 15) therefore never arise. The same at every edition. | — |

row: | DOC-A.1-17 | **CALL statement — other effects of an unsuccessful CALL whose exception condition is handled by exception processing**, §14.9.4.4 GR3h item 2, required + documented | **None beyond the transfer of control.** GR3h item 2 applies when the called program was not successfully called (EC-PROGRAM-NOT-FOUND, -PTR-NULL, -RESOURCES, -ARG-MISMATCH, -RECURSIVE-CALL or an EC-EXTERNAL condition), checking for that condition is enabled, and no ON EXCEPTION phrase is written (a NOT ON EXCEPTION phrase alone does not count). The applicable declarative runs; if it returns control with `RESUME AT NEXT STATEMENT`, execution continues after the end of the CALL statement, and the CALL has had no other effect: **no program is activated or placed in its initial state, every USING argument and the RETURNING item keep the values they held before the CALL** (`CALL "NOSUCHPG" USING X RETURNING R` leaves `X` = `"ABCD"` and `R` = 1234), NOT ON EXCEPTION is not executed, and `FUNCTION EXCEPTION-STATUS` names the condition until the next one. A declarative that ends without RESUME has no next executable statement for a fatal condition (§14.6.3), so the run unit terminates abnormally (§14.6.12). The routing is `CallEmitter`'s exception partition (kb/Work PB233). 2002 onward (the exception-condition model). | — |

row: | DOC-A.1-21 | **CHAR function — which one of the multiple characters is returned**, §15.15.4 r2 (second sentence), required + documented | The alphanumeric twin of item 22. §15.15.4 r2 has two branches and only the second is an implementor obligation. **Branch 1 — the order is DEFINED** (an `ALPHABET` literal phrase with `ALSO`): the standard answers, and COBOL.NET returns the first character defined for the position — under `ALPHABET AL IS "C" ALSO "A" ALSO "B" "D"` as the program collating sequence, `FUNCTION CHAR(FUNCTION ORD("A"))` is `"C"` (`LiteralPhraseCollation.CharAt`). **Branch 2 — the order is UNDEFINED, and this is item 21:** an `ALPHABET … IS LOCALE` sequence is an algorithm, not a written order, so every set of characters the locale collates equally shares one ordinal position with no order among its members. **COBOL.NET returns the LOWEST-CODED member of that rank** (`LocaleCollation.CharAt` reading `OrderVector.FirstOfRank`, materialized once per collator), so the answer is the same for every invocation at a given implementation, collating sequence and ordinal position: X"00", X"01" and X"1F" all share ordinal 1 of a locale sequence, and `FUNCTION CHAR(1)` is X"00". 2002 onward (the LOCALE phrase). | — |

record.notes: Verified by reading LocaleCollation.CharAt (returns OrderVector.FirstOfRank[position], the lowest code unit collating at that rank; field comment cites §15.15.4 r2) and by probes: /tmp/adj/doc/doc-w1-s1/probe/i21.cob (PROGRAM COLLATING SEQUENCE IS LOC, ALPHABET LOC IS LOCALE; --std 2002 and 2023): ORD(X"00")=ORD(X"01")=ORD(X"1F")=1, CHAR(1) -> CONVERT(..ANY ANUM HEX)=00, stable across two invocations; i21b.cob (ALPHABET AL IS "C" ALSO "A" ALSO "B" "D"; --std 85 and 2023): ORD("A")=1, CHAR(1)=C (branch 1, standard-defined; pinned separately by conformance:2002/pb59_char_representative, which does not pin this determination). No alphanumeric twin of l1_char_national_locale_tie exists, so Pinned-by is —. cite.py --check 15.15.4 'If the order of multiple characters having the same position is undefined, the implementor shall define which of those multiple characters is returned' OK (2); 12.3.7.4 'Literal-1 is the first character in the sequence ...' row: | DOC-A.1-29 | **Compile-time arithmetic — mode of arithmetic used and rules for intermediate data handling**, §7.3.6 (§7.3.6.3 GR2 · §7.3.6.2 SR2), required + documented | **A mode unique to compile-time arithmetic: .NET `System.Decimal`**, the same for a constant entry (`CONSTANT AS`), a `>>DEFINE` value and a `>>IF`/`>>EVALUATE` operand (one evaluator, `CompileTimeExpressionEvaluator`). It is neither a §8.8.1 standard mode nor the runtime's native arithmetic. **Precision and range:** each intermediate result is a decimal number of up to 28–29 significant digits (at most 28 of them after the decimal point) whose magnitude is below about 7.9×10²⁸; an intermediate result outside that range is a compile-time error — COBOLNET1547 in a constant entry, COBOLNET1619 in a directive — never a wrapped or truncated value (`9999999999999999999999999999 * 10` is refused). **Intermediate rounding:** addition, subtraction, multiplication and division are exact whenever the exact result fits those digits; otherwise the result is **rounded to the nearest representable value, a tie to the even digit** — division does NOT truncate: `2 / 3 * 3` is 2 and `100 / 7 * 7` is 100 (a truncating division would give 1 and 99), while `1 / 3 * 3` is 0; `0.0000000000000000000000000005 / 2 * 10000000000000000000000000000` is 2 and `0.0000000000000000000000000015 / 2 * 10000000000000000000000000000` is 8. **Final result:** truncated toward zero to its integer part, as §7.3.6.3 GR3 requires (`-7 / 2` is -3, `2.5 + 0` is 2). Nothing is moved to a recycle area and nothing can be recovered by the runtime. Before deleting, the file is checked in this order: **open on this connector** → `41` and nothing is deleted (GR13); the GR18 fixed-attribute match, which never fails because the validated attribute set is empty (item 50); **held open by another file connector** — one of this run unit's, or another run unit's (tested by requesting exclusive access to the file: on Windows every outstanding handle refuses it; on Linux and macOS only a handle holding an advisory lock does, which every COBOL.NET file connector's handle holds, so a POSIX unlink never destroys a file another COBOL.NET run unit has open, while a plain open handle of a non-.NET process does not block the delete) → `62` and the file is not deleted (GR15); **absent** → `05`, a successful completion with no action (GR14), and a bare `ASSIGN USING` connector that has never been associated is treated as absent without touching any file; present but not accessible → `37` (GR16); a medium that refuses deletion (a write-protected volume or read-only mount) → `37` (GR17), a sharing refusal raised by the delete itself → `62`, any other host failure → `30`. On success the status is `00` and a later OPEN INPUT of the file reports `35`. Available from COBOL-2023 (COBOLNET0900 below). Implemented in `FileRegistry.DeleteFile` over `HostFile.Probe` and `HostFile.IsHeldByAnother`; the RETRY phrase's handling of the `62` conflict is item 109's. | `conformance:2023/delete_file`; `conformance:2023/delete_file_absent`; `conformance:2023/delete_file_sharing` |

row: | DOC-A.1-61 | **Dynamic-capacity table — size, location and time of physical allocation**, §8.5.1.9 dynamic-capacity tables (§8.5.1.9.1), required + need not be documented (VOLUNTARY — kept because it explains the cost of growth) | Each `OCCURS DYNAMIC` table is **one managed array of its own, stored outside the record that contains it** (the record holds a reference to it), so growing a table never moves or resizes its containing group. **Time and size:** the array is allocated when the containing data item is created, with room for the larger of the initial current capacity and 4 occurrences — the initial capacity being the FROM integer (or 0), raised to a table VALUE's capacity — and the initial occurrences are initialized at once. It is **reallocated only when a receiving reference or a SET needs a higher capacity than the array holds** (a sending reference beyond the current capacity never allocates or grows the table), by doubling (from at least 4) until it is large enough, never beyond 1,073,741,823 occurrences; newly allocated occurrences, including every intermediate one, are initialized immediately with the element's initial value (whether or not INITIALIZED is written). **Lowering the capacity** (SET … TO / DOWN BY) releases nothing physically — the slots are kept for reuse, as the §8.5.1.9.4 NOTE permits — and an occurrence re-created by a later increase is initialized afresh, never the value it held before. Implemented in `CobolDynTable` (`GrowTo`, `SetCapacity`). ⚠ An allocation the host cannot satisfy is not yet reported as EC-BOUND-TABLE-LIMIT (kb/Work PB1410, open). | — |

row: | DOC-A.1-69 | **Fatal exception conditions — which are detected at compile time, and when**, §14.6.13.1.3, optional + need not be documented (VOLUNTARY) | **One fatal exception condition is detected at compile time: EC-ORDER-NOT-SUPPORTED.** When a SPECIAL-NAMES `ORDER TABLE ... IS literal` clause names a cultural ordering table this implementation does not provide, the compiler reports **warning COBOLNET1662** at that clause. A FUNCTION STANDARD-COMPARE that uses the table sets EC-ORDER-NOT-SUPPORTED at run time (§15.85.4). **The compiler always produces executable code**, whether checking is enabled or not. The permission §14.6.13.1.3 gives to omit code for a condition detected at compile time is never used, so detection never becomes a compile error. Nothing else is detected at compile time. A constant subscript outside the OCCURS bounds, a constant reference modification outside the item, a literal zero divisor and a constant intrinsic argument outside its domain all compile without a diagnostic. These are general rules, not syntax rules. With checking enabled the program ends at run time with the fatal condition (EC-BOUND-SUBSCRIPT, EC-BOUND-REF-MOD, EC-SIZE-ZERO-DIVIDE, EC-ARGUMENT-FUNCTION); with checking off it continues. Compile-time errors that name a run-time condition, such as COBOLNET1688 for EC-PROGRAM-ARG-MISMATCH, enforce syntax rules and are not detections under this item. The warning is `DiagnosticCatalog.OrderTableUnresolved`. | — |

row: | DOC-A.1-72 | **FILE-CONTROL entry, ASSIGN clause — consistency rules for external file connectors**, §12.4.5 GR1, required + documented | §12.4.5.3 GR1 b) requires the file control entries that reference one external file connector to have *"A consistent specification for data-name-1, device-name-1, and literal-1 in the ASSIGN clause"* and leaves the rules to the implementor. **COBOL.NET's rule: the entries must name the same file target and the same data-name-1, and nothing more.** (1) **The TO phrase is compared by the operand that names the file** (item 71), not by every word written: a leading device class is dropped, a literal is compared by its value and a device-name by its spelling. So `ASSIGN TO DISK "xa.dat"`, `ASSIGN TO PRINTER "xa.dat"` and `ASSIGN TO "xa.dat"` are consistent, and a device-name and a literal with the same spelling are the same name, so `ASSIGN TO XADAT` and `ASSIGN TO "xadat"` are consistent. Item 71's host-path mapping is NOT applied before the comparison: `ASSIGN TO XADAT` and `ASSIGN TO "xadat.txt"` are NOT consistent, although both open the host file `xadat.txt`. The comparison ignores case, so `"Data.txt"` and `"data.txt"` are consistent, even though on a case-sensitive host they name different physical files; the file opened is the one named in the program that executes the OPEN. An entry with a TO phrase and one without are not consistent. (2) **The USING data-name-1 is compared by spelling, qualifiers included, ignoring case.** `IN` and `OF` are the same, so `FNAME IN G` and `FNAME OF G` are consistent; `FNAME` and `FNAME OF G` are not, and neither are an entry with a USING phrase and one without. The check runs only when checking for EC-EXTERNAL-FILE-MISMATCH is enabled. It happens when a second program that describes the external file is activated: the two ASSIGN fields are part of the `SelectFingerprint` each program registers with `ExternalStore.Describe` (built in `OoEmitter.EmitExternalDescribes`), and a difference raises **EC-EXTERNAL-FILE-MISMATCH** (§14.8.4.4), which is fatal. **⛔ The two programs still hold SEPARATE STORAGE for an identically-spelled data-name-1, and that is deliberate.** §12.4.5.3 GR3 b) associates the connector with the file named *"in the runtime element that executes the OPEN, SORT, or MERGE statement"*, which only makes sense if the entries MAY name different data items. GR1 i) shows how the standard words it when it wants the opposite (FILE STATUS: *"where data-name-4 shall reference the same corresponding external data item"*), and §13.4.5.4 GR2 c) 2. does the same for LINAGE; GR1 b) says neither. Implemented at `FileConnector.Associate`, called with the executing program's own rendered specification (kb/Work PB673). | — |

row: | DOC-A.1-74 | **Figurative constant values — representation of ZERO, SPACE and QUOTE**, §8.3.3.6 (§8.3.3.6.4 GR1), required + documented | Each has ONE representation, the same code unit in both coded character sets (both are UTF-16, one code unit per character position — item 33): **SPACE is U+0020, ZERO is U+0030 (the character '0'), QUOTE is U+0022 (the character '"')**. In an alphanumeric item that is the one-byte DISPLAY image 0x20 / 0x30 / 0x22 (item 209); in a national item it is the two-byte code unit 0x0020 / 0x0030 / 0x0022 (two bytes per national position, as item 209's row states). So, with no PROGRAM COLLATING SEQUENCE, `MOVE SPACE` to a `PIC X` item gives `FUNCTION ORD` 33, ZERO 49, QUOTE 35, and the national item gives the same values (ORD reports the position in the program collating sequence, so under `PROGRAM COLLATING SEQUENCE IS` an EBCDIC alphabet it reports 65 for SPACE although the stored character is still U+0020); `SPACE = X"20"`, `QUOTE = X"22"`, `ZERO = X"30"` and `QUOTE = NX"0022"` are all true. Neither a PROGRAM COLLATING SEQUENCE, an ALPHABET clause nor a CODE-SET clause changes these values in storage; those clauses affect comparison order and the file's external code set only. The single source for the fill characters is `FigurativeConstants.FillChar`. (A BOOLEAN receiver is outside this item: ZERO fills it with the boolean character '0', and so does SPACE, determination D-B2 in §3.) | — |

row: | DOC-A.1-76 | **File sharing — which devices allow concurrent access to a physical file**, §9.1.15, required + documented | **All of them.** Every physical file is a path in the host file system: a regular file, or a device path such as `/dev/null` that the host opens as a file. The device classes `DISK` and `PRINTER` both name such a file (item 71). COBOL.NET treats every physical file as one that allows concurrent access, so it is *shareable* in the sense of §14.9.27.4 GR21 and the SHARING clause and SHARING phrase always apply. A second connector's OPEN of the same file is decided by §9.1.15 Table 19: connectors that both specify `SHARING WITH ALL OTHER` (with `LOCK MODE MANUAL`) can be open on one regular file or on `/dev/null` at the same time, each with status 00, and a `SHARING WITH NO OTHER` OPEN of a file another connector has open fails with 61. `ASSIGN TO PRINTER "f"` and `ASSIGN TO DISK "f"` are the same shareable file. This row covers only which files can be shared. How strongly the file lock excludes other run units depends on the host, and that is open under kb/Work PB833. The mode used when no sharing mode is specified (item 77) is open under kb/Work PB322. Implemented by `FileRegistry.SharedOpenAttempt` and `PhysicalFileTable`, which apply Table 19 to every connector without testing the device. | — |

row: | DOC-A.1-78 | **Fixed file attributes — whether the ability to share a physical file is a fixed file attribute**, §9.1.6, required + documented | **No.** A physical file records nothing about sharing. The sharing mode belongs to each FILE CONNECTOR: it comes from that connector's SHARING clause, or from the SHARING phrase of the OPEN that opens it (§14.9.27.4 GR21–GR23). It is set when the OPEN succeeds and checked against the connectors that have the same physical file open at that moment (§9.1.15 Table 19). When the connector is closed, its sharing mode is gone. So a file created through a `SHARING WITH NO OTHER` connector can later be opened through two `SHARING WITH ALL OTHER` connectors at once, and both OPENs succeed with 00. While the NO OTHER connector is open, any other OPEN of the file fails with 61, and the NO OTHER connector's own OPEN fails with 61 while other connectors have the file open. This is also why A.1 item 129's validated fixed attributes never include sharing. Implemented by `FileRegistry.RegisterSharing` (the per-connector mode) and `FileRegistry.SharedOpenAttempt` (the check at OPEN). | — |

row: | DOC-A.1-94 | **GOBACK statement — constraints on the value in the STATUS phrase**, §14.9.18.3 GR10 (printed as §14.9.18.4 GR10 in this text), required + documented | **No value is refused. The STATUS operand becomes the process exit code**, with the same mapping as STOP (A.1 item 192, §3 'STOP RUN / GOBACK termination status'). The syntax rules still apply: identifier-2 must be an integer data item or a data item of usage display or national (§14.9.18.3 SR6), and a numeric literal-1 must be an integer (SR7). The mapping is: **(1)** a numeric operand's integer value is the exit code (a data item's value truncated toward zero); **(2)** a non-numeric operand (an alphanumeric or national item, a non-numeric literal, a figurative constant) is decoded as an unsigned integer from its digit characters, and a position that is not a digit adds no digit, so `STATUS "007"` exits 7, `STATUS "A1B2"` exits 12 and `STATUS "ABEND"` or `STATUS SPACE` exits 0 (`CobolNum.FromAlphanumeric`); **(3)** the host then keeps what it can report: the value is narrowed to a 32-bit integer and a POSIX host keeps only the low 8 bits, so `STATUS 300` exits 44 and `STATUS -3` exits 253. With no STATUS value, `GOBACK WITH ERROR` exits 1 and `WITH NORMAL` (or no phrase) exits 0; a STATUS value, when present, wins over ERROR or NORMAL. The value reaches the operating system only when the GOBACK ends the run unit, that is, in a main program (§14.9.18.4 GR3); in a called program the GOBACK returns to its caller and the status is not used. The phrase is COBOL-2023 only: at `--std 2014` and below it is refused with COBOLNET0900. Implemented by `CallBinder.DecodeGobackPhrases` and the `RunUnit.ExitStatus` setter. | `conformance-test:StopGobackExitCodeTests.TerminationStatus_SetsProcessExitCode`; `conformance-test:StopGobackExitCodeTests.NonNumericStatusOperand_IsLegalAndInterpretedNumerically` |

row: | DOC-A.1-118 | **Locale specification — how the user default and system default locales are defined**, §8.2.1, required — A.1 says this need not be documented, and it is documented here anyway because the environment variables are the user's only control over the defaults | Both defaults are decided **once per run unit, when the run unit starts** (`LocaleState`, created with the `RunUnit`), and they are always two separate settings. **User default locale:** the environment variable **`COBOL_USER_LOCALE`** if it is set; otherwise the process's current .NET culture (`CultureInfo.CurrentCulture`, which on Unix follows `LANG`/`LC_ALL`); otherwise the root locale. **System default locale:** the environment variable **`COBOL_SYSTEM_LOCALE`** if it is set; otherwise the host's installed UI culture (`CultureInfo.InstalledUICulture`); otherwise the root locale. The variables' values are locale names in the item-119 notation, trimmed; `C`, `POSIX`, `root` or `INVARIANT` names the root locale. **At least one user default and one system default always exist**: in an environment with no locale data at all (.NET invariant globalization), both fall back to the root locale and the run unit starts normally. The current locale starts as the user default for every category (§14.6.6). A program can change the user default for the rest of the run unit with `SET LOCALE USER-DEFAULT TO …`, but it cannot change the system default (§8.2.1: the capability is not provided), so `LocaleState.SystemDefault` has no setter. Example: with `COBOL_USER_LOCALE=de-DE` and `COBOL_SYSTEM_LOCALE=fr-FR`, `FUNCTION LOCALE-DATE("20260924")` gives `24.09.2026` after `SET LOCALE LC_ALL TO USER-DEFAULT` and `24/09/2026` after `SET LOCALE LC_ALL TO SYSTEM-DEFAULT`. row: | DOC-A.1-119 | **Locale specification — manner of implementation**, §8.2.1, required — A.1 says this need not be documented, and it is documented here anyway because it decides which locale names a program may use | **A locale is named by a BCP 47 / CLDR language tag**, and POSIX-style spellings are accepted and normalized: `es_ES.UTF-8` is `es-ES`, `de-DE@phonebook` is `de-DE` with the phonebook collation, and `C`, `POSIX`, `root`, `INVARIANT` and the empty name are the **root locale** (`LocaleIdentification.Normalize`). **A locale is available** when COBOL.NET has CLDR collation data for it, a site tailoring names it, or .NET recognizes it as a culture (`LocaleIdentification.IsAvailable`). A name that is none of these, such as `xx-NOWHERE`, is not available (EC-LOCALE-MISSING when a program selects it with checking on). The run unit keeps a current locale for **each of the six categories**, LC_COLLATE, LC_CTYPE, LC_MESSAGES, LC_MONETARY, LC_NUMERIC and LC_TIME, each set independently by SET LOCALE (`LocaleState`). **LC_COLLATE never comes from the host**: it is COBOL.NET's own collation table generated from Unicode CLDR release 48-2 / UCA 17.0.0 data, so a locale orders text the same way on every host. **LC_CTYPE, LC_MONETARY and LC_TIME** content comes from the nearest predefined .NET culture: the tag, then its parents (`sr-Latn-RS`, then `sr-Latn`, then `sr`) (`LocaleFacts`). When no ancestor is a .NET culture, or the process runs in .NET invariant-globalization mode, that content is incomplete: the invariant culture's values stand in, and an operation that needs the category sets EC-LOCALE-INVALID when checking is on. The implementor default when the environment supplies none is the root locale (item 118). COBOL-2002 onward. | `unit:LocaleStateTests.ExternalIdentification_IsNormalized_PerDeterminationL1`; `unit:LocaleStateTests.Availability_IsTheOneKnownLocaleRule`; `unit:LocaleStateTests.Set_SwitchesOnlyTheNamedCategories_AndTheyPersist` |

row: | DOC-A.1-120 | **Locale switch — whether a switch of the current locale by a non-COBOL runtime module is recognized by COBOL**, §8.2.1, conditionally required (documented if provided) | **No, for every category.** COBOL.NET never activates a non-COBOL module (a CALL cannot reach one, item 19). The only non-COBOL code that can share a run unit's process is a .NET host that activates a COBOL program, together with anything that host runs. The run unit reads the process culture **once, when it starts**, to determine its user and system default locales (item 118). After that, every locale-dependent operation uses only the run unit's own per-category state (`LocaleState`), and only SET LOCALE changes it. A later change of `CultureInfo.CurrentCulture`, `CultureInfo.DefaultThreadCurrentCulture` or the process's `LANG` by non-COBOL code is not utilized for LC_COLLATE, LC_CTYPE, LC_MESSAGES, LC_MONETARY, LC_NUMERIC or LC_TIME. Operations that are not locale-dependent never consult the process culture: DISPLAY of a floating-point or numeric item, NUMVAL and UPPER-CASE give the same result under `LANG=de_DE.UTF-8` or `tr_TR.UTF-8` as under `LANG=C`. A host that wants a different locale sets `COBOL_USER_LOCALE` (or its culture) before the run unit starts. COBOL-2002 onward. | — |

row: | DOC-A.1-122 | **National literals — number of hexadecimal digits that map to a national character**, §8.3.3.5.3 SR5, required + documented | **FOUR.** Each group of four hexadecimal digits in an `NX"…"` (or `NX'…'`) literal is one national character: the UTF-16 code unit with that value, which is also one national character position. `NX"004100420043"` is the three characters `ABC`, `FUNCTION LENGTH(NX"00410042")` is 2, and `FUNCTION ORD(NX"00E9")` is 234 (é is U+00E9). A character outside the Basic Multilingual Plane is written as its two surrogate code units and occupies two positions: `LENGTH(NX"D83DDE00")` is 2. A literal whose digit count is not a multiple of four, such as `NX"414"` or `NX"004100"`, is rejected with **COBOLNET1635** (`CobolLiteral.HexGroupViolation`). NX literals exist from COBOL-2002 on; at COBOL-85 they are COBOLNET0900. The check is not yet made for an NX argument of an intrinsic function written without the FUNCTION keyword (kb/Work PB1393). | `conformance:2023/r03_hexadecimal_national_and_boolean_literals` |

row: | DOC-A.1-130 | **OPEN statement with the OUTPUT phrase — positioning of the output file with regard to physical page boundaries**, §14.9.27.4 GR18, required + documented | Physical pages have meaning for a **sequential-organization** file (record sequential or LINE SEQUENTIAL) — the files WRITE ... ADVANCING and the LINAGE clause apply to; a relative or indexed file has no pages. **OPEN OUTPUT creates the host file empty and places the output medium at its first byte, which is the TOP OF THE FIRST PHYSICAL PAGE.** The OPEN itself writes nothing — no form feed, no blank lines, no margin: a file opened OUTPUT and closed with no WRITE is **0 bytes** (`SequentialConnector.OpenWriter`). **No LINAGE clause:** because the medium is already at a page top, the first `WRITE ... AFTER ADVANCING PAGE` (or BEFORE) still repositions to the NEXT physical page as §14.9.51.4 GR25 h) says, by writing a form feed (U+000C) — so a file whose first WRITE advances PAGE begins with a form feed (`SequentialConnector.Advance`). **LINAGE clause:** at the completion of the OPEN the device is on line 1 of the first logical page, and that logical page begins at the file's first line; LINAGE-COUNTER is 1 (§13.18.34.4 GR7). The logical page's TOP margin lines are written onto the medium immediately before the first record is presented — never by the OPEN, so a LINAGE file closed with no WRITE is also 0 bytes (`SequentialConnector.BeginLinagePage`, `EmitTopMarginIfPending`). Example: `FD F LINAGE 5 FOOTING 4 TOP 2 BOTTOM 1`, OPEN OUTPUT, one plain `WRITE` of `AAA` gives two empty lines, then `AAA` (line terminator per item 114). Same in every edition. | `conformance:2023/pb523_linage_margins_on_the_medium`; `conformance:85/pb523_linage_margins_on_the_medium_85` |

row: | DOC-A.1-138 | **Parameterized classes and interfaces — manner and time of expansion**, §7.1 (with §12.3.8.4 GR5 / GR8), required + need not be documented (documented voluntarily) | **Time:** a parameterized class or interface is expanded at compile time, once per compilation group, AFTER all text manipulation — COPY, REPLACE and the compiler directives have finished, the source has been parsed, and expansion runs at the start of binding (`OoExpansion.Expand`, called from `BinderDriver`). So a REPLACE that produces a formal parameter's name inside the definition takes part in the substitution. **Manner:** each distinct expansion (`CLASS new-name EXPANDS definition USING actual …` or the interface form in a REPOSITORY paragraph) becomes an ORDINARY class or interface: the definition's own tokens re-parsed with every occurrence of each formal parameter replaced by its actual parameter (§12.3.8.4 GR5 / GR8) and the header renamed to the expansion's name. It is never a .NET generic type, and from binding onward an expansion cannot be told from a written class — its FACTORY and OBJECT data are its own (two expansions of one definition keep separate factory counters). The parameterized definition itself generates nothing. **Identity (§9.3.12):** specifiers that repeat one (expansion name, definition, actual parameters) triple, in one or several source elements, create ONE class; reusing an expansion name with a different definition or different actuals is **COBOLNET2240**. row: | DOC-A.1-139 | **PERFORM statement — whether location information is available when the LOCATION phrase is not specified**, §14.9.28.4 GR14 (through §7.3.25.4 GR7), required + documented | **Not available.** An exception-checking PERFORM (Format 3, `PERFORM … WHEN exception-name …  END-PERFORM`) enables the exception conditions its WHEN phrases name over imperative-statement-1 through an implicit TURN directive (§14.9.28.4 GR14), and that implicit directive carries LOCATION exactly when the PERFORM writes `WITH LOCATION`. Without it COBOL.NET saves no location information for a condition raised there — the same determination as the explicit `>>TURN` directive (item 204), so neither route yields location data the other withholds. Consequence inside the WHEN handler and after the PERFORM: `FUNCTION EXCEPTION-LOCATION` returns one alphanumeric space, `FUNCTION EXCEPTION-LOCATION-N` one national space and `FUNCTION EXCEPTION-STATEMENT` 63 spaces, while `FUNCTION EXCEPTION-STATUS` still names the condition. With `PERFORM WITH LOCATION` the full location is produced — e.g. `PL; MAIN-P; 12` and statement `RAISE`. ⛔ **An explicit TURN that already enables the name wins, in both directions:** §14.9.28.4 GR14 assumes the implicit TURN only "if checking … is not enabled for imperative-statement-1 by a TURN directive", so when a `>>TURN … CHECKING ON` in force before the PERFORM already enables a name its WHEN phrase lists, no implicit directive is assumed for that name and THAT directive's LOCATION setting governs — under `>>TURN EC-USER-X1 CHECKING ON WITH LOCATION` a PERFORM without LOCATION still yields `PL2; MAIN-P; 7`, and under `>>TURN EC-USER-X1 CHECKING ON` (no LOCATION) a `PERFORM WITH LOCATION` yields one space. The LOCATION flag travels on `BoundExceptionPerform.WithLocation` into `TurnState.WithImplicitEnable`. COBOL 2023 only (Format 3 PERFORM is COBOLNET0900 in earlier editions). | `conformance:2023/l1_exception_no_location_arms`; `conformance:2023/exception_statement_ambient` |

row: | DOC-A.1-141 | **Procedure division header rules when the activating or the activated runtime element is not COBOL — restrictions and mechanisms (parameter matching, data type representation, returning of a value, omission of parameters)**, §14.2.3 GR13, conditionally required + documented | **Supported non-COBOL language products: any .NET language, and only as the ACTIVATING element.** No non-COBOL element can be ACTIVATED: there is no CALL-CONVENTION directive (item 19), and a CALL, a program-pointer or `ADDRESS OF PROGRAM` resolves only COBOL.NET programs (otherwise EC-PROGRAM-NOT-FOUND). **Mechanism:** every generated program class implements `ICobolProgram`, and a .NET host activates the program as a called program through `ICobolProgram.Call(CobolArg[] args, CobolArg? returning)`. **Parameter matching:** positional, `args[0]` to the first USING formal and so on (§14.2.3 GR2) — never by name. A trailing formal with no argument is OMITTED; an argument beyond the last formal is ignored; this entry performs no argument-count check (EC-PROGRAM-ARG-MISMATCH for a count is raised only for a COBOL CALL, in `ProgramTable.CallProgram`). **Data type representation:** each argument is a `CobolArg(Mode, Carrier, Num, Layout)`. `Carrier` is a `ManagedPointer<T>` over the host's own storage: a `ManagedPointer<string>` holding the item's character image (one UTF-16 character per character position) for an alphanumeric, national, edited or group formal, or a native numeric cell (`long`, `Int128`, `double`, …) whose representation `Num` (a `NumProfile`: digits, scale, sign and usage) describes; `Layout` describes a group that contains a table. A formal of another shape sees the carrier through a converting view of the SAME storage (§14.2.3 GR8), so the program's stores reach the host's storage. `Mode` makes no copy: a COBOL CALL builds the BY CONTENT copy on the activating side, so a host that wants BY CONTENT passes a carrier over a copy it owns; a BY VALUE formal always adopts a detached copy (§14.2.3 GR10). A carrier the formal cannot read fails the activation with the .NET exception `CobolCallException` whose `EcName` is EC-PROGRAM-ARG-MISMATCH, before any statement of the program runs (`CobolArgAdapt`). **Omission of parameters:** pass `ManagedPointer.Null` as the carrier, or pass fewer arguments; the omitted-argument condition is then true (§14.9.4.4 GR11), a reference raises EC-PROGRAM-ARG-OMITTED when checking for it is enabled in the program (GR12), and otherwise reads an empty value (zero for a numeric formal). **Returning of a value:** the RETURNING item's content is delivered into the `returning` argument's carrier, described by that `CobolArg` exactly as a COBOL receiver is; GOBACK / EXIT PROGRAM is an ordinary method return to the host (§3, "Return to a NON-COBOL activating runtime element"). Same in every edition. | — |

row: | DOC-A.1-153 | **Record locking — the default mode when the user specifies none**, §12.4.5.9.4 GR1 b) 2., required + documented | **No record locking** — the third option GR1 b) 2. names. A file connector whose file control entry has neither a LOCK MODE clause nor a SHARING clause, opened by an OPEN with no SHARING phrase, SETS NO RECORD LOCKS: a READ does not lock, and an explicit `WITH LOCK` phrase on its I-O statements obtains nothing (`FileRegistry.ImplementorDefaultShare`, lock mode `FileLockMode.None`). It still RESPECTS other connectors' locks, because §9.1.16 makes a locked record inaccessible to every other file connector: its READ, REWRITE and DELETE of a record another connector has locked are refused with I-O status `51`, and READ … IGNORING LOCK reads it. Example (that two clause-less connectors can have the file open at the same time is the DEFAULT SHARING MODE, item 131, which is not yet determined — kb/Work PB322; the example shows the lock behaviour only): two such connectors on one relative file — A `READ … WITH LOCK` record 1 (`00`), B READs and REWRITEs record 1 (`00`, `00`); a third connector with `LOCK MODE IS AUTOMATIC` READs record 1 and locks it, and B's next READ of record 1 is `51`. COBOL 2002 and later. | `conformance:2002/pb669_lock_visibility_plain_connector` |

row: | DOC-A.1-154 | **Record locking — the maximum number of record locks a run unit may hold**, §12.4.5.9.4 GR7, required + documented | **255** — the standard's minimum (`PhysicalFileTable.RunUnitLockMax`). The count is every record lock held by every file connector of the run unit, over all physical files. An I-O statement that would obtain a 256th lock is unsuccessful with I-O status **`53`** (§9.1.13.8 item 3) and obtains no lock; a WRITE or REWRITE refused this way changes no record (the ceiling is checked before the record is touched, `PhysicalFileTable.PreflightNewLock`). Re-locking a record the same connector already holds does not count again. When the connector's own ceiling (item 155) is also reached, `54` is reported. COBOL 2002 and later. | `unit:CobolFileLockTests.RunUnitLockLimit_256thRunUnitLock_Is53` |

row: | DOC-A.1-155 | **Record locks — the maximum number of record locks one file connector may hold**, §12.4.5.9.4 GR7, required + documented | **15** — the standard's minimum (`PhysicalFileTable.ConnectorLockMax`). Only a connector with multiple record locking (`LOCK ON MULTIPLE RECORDS`) can hold more than one lock (GR6), and the MULTIPLE phrase is not allowed for sequential organization or access (§12.4.5.9.3 SR2), so the ceiling is reachable on relative and indexed files with random or dynamic access. An I-O statement that would obtain a 16th lock for the connector is unsuccessful with I-O status **`54`** (§9.1.13.8 item 4), obtains no lock and — for a READ — is an unsuccessful READ like any other (§14.9.30.4 GR18): no record position is established, so the next sequential READ is `46`, never the record after the refused one; a WRITE or REWRITE refused this way changes no record (`PhysicalFileTable.PreflightNewLock`). Re-locking a record the connector already holds does not count again; UNLOCK and CLOSE release its locks. COBOL 2002 and later. | `conformance:2023/pb338_read_lock_limit_position`; `unit:CobolFileLockTests.ConnectorLockLimit_16thRecord_Is54` |

Golden 2023/pb338_read_lock_limit_position: READ 16 under LOCK ON MULTIPLE = 54 on relative, indexed and random legs, then UNLOCK 00 and the next READ NEXT is 46 (§14.9.30.4 GR18: no valid record position after an unsuccessful READ) - pins the value and the status; unit ConnectorLockLimit_16thRecord_Is54 pins the ceiling directly. record.notes: A.1 item 156 (cite.py --check A.1 -> OK §A.1 156): required + documented (A.1 cites 'Clause 6, Reference format, rule 3b'). §6.1: 'The implementor shall specify any control characters that terminate a free-form line' (cite.py --check 6.1 -> OK §6.1 b)). docs/CONFORMANCE.md §7 has NO DOC-A.1-156 row (the only reference-format row is DOC-A.1-158, margin R) and no prose elsewhere names the free-form line terminators. Code: NormalizeToFreeFormMapped splits the source on '\n' and each free-form segment line is TrimEnd('\r') (ReferenceFormatProcessor.cs:108/172), so LF terminates a line and a CR immediately before it is dropped; no other control character (FF, VT, lone CR) is a terminator. A fixed answer exists but is undocumented => DIVERGES, harm silent. Editions: free-form reference format exists from 2002 (Annex E). Owning note kb/Work PB1496 (open; its title names item 156 and its fixer owes the DOC-A.1-156 row) — cited, not re-reported. || Writer (doc-w1-s5): OMIT - re-probe CONTRADICTS the staged determination 'no other control character (lone CR) is a terminator': the free-form line terminator is not ONE rule. The preprocessor (ReferenceFormatProcessor.NormalizeToFreeFormMapped, directive recognition) splits lines on LF only, but the lexer ends a floating comment and a literal at a lone CR (CobolLexer.g4 COMMENT_TEXT ~[\r\n]+, STR_BODY). probe/cr3.cob, cr4.cob: 'DISPLAY "A" *> comment<CR>DISPLAY "B"' runs both A and B (the CR ended the comment); probe/cr5.cob: 'DISPLAY "A"<CR>>>DEFINE X AS 1' -> COBOL0307 unexpected '>' (the CR did NOT start a new line for the directive facility). FF and VT inside a line are COBOL0307 (cr1/cr2), i.e. not terminators. New defect proposed; PB1496 (open) owes the row once one rule exists.

defect.mechanism: Two stages answer 'what terminates a free-form line' differently: the reference-format/directive stage splits on LF only (CR before LF trimmed), while the lexer treats a lone CR as a line end for floating comments and literals. A lone CR therefore ends a *> comment but a >> directive after it is not at a line start.
defect.expected_from_spec: §6.1 3) b): the implementor shall specify THE control characters that terminate a free-form line - one set, applied by every stage (a line is a line for comments, literals and compiler directives alike).
defect.observed: cr3: comment ended at lone CR (B displayed); cr5: '>>DEFINE' after lone CR -> COBOL0307 unexpected '>'.

refuter.reason: Spot-check: Re-ran refute-probe/cr5.cob: lone CR before >>DEFINE -> COBOL0307 unexpected '>', while cr3.cob shows a lone CR ends a *> comment (A/B/C). row: | DOC-A.1-170 | **SEARCH ALL statement — varying of the search index during the search operation**, §14.9.37 GR9 (§14.9.37.4), required + need not be documented (VOLUNTARY) | **A forward scan in occurrence order.** The initial setting of the search index is ignored: SEARCH ALL sets it to occurrence **1**, evaluates the WHEN condition, and on a false result advances it by one, until a WHEN is satisfied or the last element has been tested (`ControlFlowEmitter.EmitAllScan`). The bound is the table's maximum occurrence count, the CURRENT count of an OCCURS DEPENDING ON table, or the current capacity of an OCCURS DYNAMIC table. The last-element test happens BEFORE the advance, so the index never holds a value outside 1 through the last element — also on an unsuccessful search, where the AT END phrase sees it at the last element tested; an empty table (current count 0) is unsuccessful with no element tested and the index at 1. On success the index holds the occurrence number of the element that satisfied the WHEN. No binary search is performed, so a table whose ASCENDING/DESCENDING KEY data is not actually in sequence still finds an element that satisfies the condition when one exists. GR9 makes the final setting after an unsuccessful search undefined, so a program shall not rely on which in-range value is left. | `conformance:85/pb447_search_all_index_stays_in_table` |

row: | DOC-A.1-181 | **SPECIAL-NAMES paragraph — allowable locale-names and literal values of the LOCALE clause**, §12.3.7 GR5 (§12.3.7.4), optional (documented if provided) | **Provided (2002 and later).** `LOCALE locale-name-1 IS {external-locale-name-1 or literal-4}` accepts the SAME set of identifications in both forms: a **locale tag** — any BCP-47 tag of a CLDR locale or of a culture .NET recognizes (`fr-FR`, `de-CH`, `sr-Latn-RS`, `zh-Hant`), a `-u-` extension allowed — or the root locale spelled `INVARIANT`, `ROOT`, `C`, `POSIX` or `und`. A **POSIX spelling** `ll_CC[.codeset][@modifier]` is normalized before use (`LocaleIdentification.Normalize`): underscores become hyphens, a `.codeset` suffix is ignored (the repertoire is always UTF-16), an `@modifier` that names a CLDR collation type becomes the `-u-co-<type>` extension (`de_DE@phonebook` is `de-DE-u-co-phonebook`), and any other modifier leaves a tag that names no locale. So `fr_FR`, `fr-FR`, `"fr_FR.UTF-8"` and `"fr-FR"` identify the same locale; the comparison is case-insensitive. The word form is limited to what a COBOL word can spell (no `.` or `@`), so `.codeset` and `@modifier` spellings need the literal form. literal-4 shall be an alphanumeric or national literal (or a concatenation expression of that class), neither zero-length nor a symbolic-character figurative constant (§12.3.7.3 SR10/SR11, `COBOLNET0898`; ⚠ today every figurative constant, SPACE included, is also refused with `COBOLNET0898`, which §8.3.3.6.3 SR1 does not permit — an open defect, kb/Work PB1537); a locale-name declared twice is `COBOLNET1665`. **Availability is decided at RUN time, never at compile time**: any spelling compiles, and a locale that is not available (`LocaleIdentification.IsAvailable` — the root, a locale with CLDR collation data, a site `.tailor` file, or a culture .NET recognizes) raises `EC-LOCALE-MISSING` at the statement that uses it when that check is enabled; with the check not enabled the statement proceeds with the root locale's conventions (a `LOCALE-DATE` through an unavailable `"zz_QQ"` or `"fr_FR@euro"` formats as `09/24/2026`, exactly as `INVARIANT` does). row: | DOC-A.1-197 | **SYNCHRONIZED clause — positioning when neither RIGHT nor LEFT is specified**, §13.18.55 GR3 (§13.18.55.4), required + documented | **The item is positioned exactly where it would be without the clause: it begins at the byte immediately after the preceding item.** COBOL.NET treats every byte position as a natural boundary — a record is a typed .NET structure, not an addressable byte buffer, so an unaligned binary item costs no extra machine operations — and therefore performs no positioning, adds no slack bytes, and does not change the size of the item or of any containing group or REDEFINES (item 195). row: | DOC-A.1-198 | **System-names — rules for the formation of a system-name**, §8.3.2.3 (§8.3.2.3.1), optional (documented if provided) | **Provided — one restriction.** A system-name is formed as any COBOL word of the target edition — letters, digits, hyphen, and (2002 and later) underscore, not beginning or ending with a hyphen or underscore (`ABC-` is a syntax error), at most 30 characters (COBOL-85), 31 (2002 and 2014) or 63 (2023), the length limit being `COBOLNET1567` — with ONE added restriction: a system-name shall not consist of digits only, because such a character-string is always read as an integer literal (`OBJECT-COMPUTER. 12345.` is a syntax error, `COBOL0001`). row: | DOC-A.1-220 | **Variable-length data items — actual time when the resources used are freed**, §8.5.1.11.3, required + need not be documented (VOLUNTARY) | **Whenever the .NET garbage collector reclaims them — a time the program cannot observe and COBOL.NET does not fix.** No variable-length item has storage of its own to release: a DYNAMIC LENGTH elementary item is a managed .NET string, so the old value becomes unreachable when a new value is stored (a MOVE of "XY" over "ABCDEFGHIJ" leaves an item of length 2), and the collector reclaims it later. A dynamic-capacity table (`OCCURS DYNAMIC`, `CobolDynTable`) holds its occurrences in a managed array that grows by doubling and is NEVER shrunk: lowering the capacity (`SET … TO`, `DOWN BY`) only lowers the current count, keeping the removed occurrences' storage until the table is enlarged again — when each re-created occurrence is created afresh as a new occurrence, never with the value it held before — or until the table itself becomes unreachable. Freeing never affects a program's results. DYNAMIC LENGTH items and dynamic-capacity tables exist from 2014 on (`COBOLNET0900` below). | — |
